Answers to what people ask most.

View all questions (/faq)

A regular eye exam focuses on diagnosing conditions and prescribing glasses or contacts. A low vision exam goes further—it evaluates how your remaining vision functions in real tasks like reading, cooking, or navigating outdoors. A low vision specialist tests contrast sensitivity, visual fields, glare tolerance, and reading speed, then recommends devices, lighting strategies, and rehabilitation services tailored to your goals.

Coverage varies significantly. Medicare typically covers the low vision exam under certain provider types but does not cover optical magnifiers or most electronic aids. Some Medicaid programs and state vocational rehabilitation agencies do cover devices. Veterans may qualify for devices through VA low vision programs. Private insurance is inconsistent—prior authorization and documentation of medical necessity are often required. Our Coverage & Funding section walks through options step by step.

It depends on your insurance and state. Many Medicare patients can self-refer to optometrists or ophthalmologists who specialize in low vision. Some insurance plans require a referral from a primary care provider or general eye doctor. Vocational rehabilitation and blind services agencies typically accept direct applications. When in doubt, call your insurer or the specialist's office directly—they can tell you exactly what documentation you need.

Students with visual impairments are entitled to a free, appropriate public education under IDEA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. A Teacher of the Visually Impaired (TVI) provides specialized instruction, and an Orientation & Mobility (O&M) specialist helps with safe navigation. Start by requesting an educational evaluation from your school district. Our School & Learning section has a checklist of what to ask for and how to advocate for the right services.

sections.heading: Our Commitment
sections.text:
Low Vision Navigator is designed to meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA accessibility guidelines. We are committed to ensuring that people with visual impairments—and all disabilities—can access and use this platform fully.

- Semantic HTML and proper heading structure throughout

- ARIA labels and roles for interactive elements

- Keyboard navigation for all menus, forms, and cards

- Visible focus indicators on all interactive elements

- Sufficient color contrast (minimum 4.5:1 for text)

- Forms include visible labels and inline error messages

- Reduced motion support for users who prefer it

- Skip to main content link at top of every page

sections.heading: Keyboard Navigation
sections.text:
Tab Move focus to next interactive element
Shift + Tab Move focus to previous element
Enter / Space Activate button or link
Escape Close menus and modals
Arrow Keys Navigate within grouped controls
Home / End Jump to first/last item in a list

sections.heading: Screen Reader Tips
sections.text:
- Use the "Skip to main content" link (first element, visible on focus) to bypass navigation.

- Headings are structured H1 > H2 > H3 for logical document outline navigation.

- All images have descriptive alt text; decorative images are marked presentation role.

- Form inputs have visible labels and are linked via aria-labelledby.

- Error messages are announced via aria-live regions.

- Mega menus respond to keyboard navigation and Escape to close.

Low Vision Navigator's content is developed and reviewed with input from practicing low vision clinicians.

Our advisory board is composed of practicing clinicians from across the low vision rehabilitation spectrum. Their role is to review content for clinical accuracy, flag outdated guidance, and ensure that the practical realities of low vision care are accurately represented.
Advisory board members are not paid for listings or referrals. They participate to improve the quality of information available to people navigating vision loss—a population that is consistently underserved by general health information resources.

sections.heading: How We Review Resources
sections.text:
Our editorial process for vetting, publishing, and maintaining listings on Low Vision Navigator.

Low Vision Navigator is a health information resource. The accuracy and clinical relevance of our listings directly affect people making real decisions about their care. This page describes our review process in full.
We do not accept payment for placement. Organizations cannot buy their way into our directory. Listings are included because they meet our editorial criteria—not because they have a marketing relationship with us.

sections.heading: Initial vetting
sections.text:
Every organization submitted or identified for inclusion is checked against three criteria: (1) it provides a service directly relevant to people with low vision or blindness; (2) it has verifiable contact information and a functioning website or phone number; and (3) it is an established organization—not a commercial listing, SEO page, or affiliate referral.

- 2

sections.heading: Accreditation and credential check
sections.text:
For clinical providers, we check for relevant licensure (optometry, ophthalmology, OT, COMS) at the state level and note whether the organization holds accreditation from bodies such as CARF International or the Commission on Accreditation of Rehabilitation Facilities. For blind services agencies, we verify enrollment in the state VR system and federal funding status.

- 3

sections.heading: Coverage and service scope review
sections.text:
We document what the organization actually offers—clinical, rehabilitation, financial assistance, peer support, technology lending, etc.—and cross-reference against published service descriptions, program guides, or direct outreach. We note virtual availability, referral requirements, cost structure, and whether services are open to self-referrals.

- 4

sections.heading: Clinical advisory review
sections.text:
Listings in specialized categories (low vision clinics, rehabilitation programs, assistive technology providers) are reviewed by a member of our clinical advisory board before publication. The advisory board is composed of practicing low vision optometrists, vision rehabilitation therapists, orientation & mobility specialists, and assistive technology instructors.

- 5

sections.heading: Ongoing monitoring
sections.text: We re-verify active listings at least annually, and more frequently for organizations with high traffic. We also accept flagged corrections from users—any listing can be reported via our contact page. Flagged listings are reviewed and updated or removed within 5 business days.

sections.heading: Coverage and funding information
sections.text: Our coverage, billing, and policy content (Medicare, Medicaid, VA benefits, state programs) is reviewed separately from directory listings. Policy content is reviewed against official CMS, SSA, and VA documentation, and is updated when regulations or coverage determinations change. Our clinical advisory board reviews the clinical framing of policy guidance before publication.

sections.heading: What we don't include
sections.text:
- ✕ Commercial retailers without a clinical or rehabilitation component

- ✕ Affiliate links or paid promotional listings

- ✕ Organizations with unresolved complaints or active regulatory actions

- ✕ Listings with unverifiable contact information

- ✕ Programs that have closed, paused enrollment, or are no longer accepting referrals (when known)

sections.heading: Report an issue
sections.text: If you find an inaccurate listing, a closed organization, or missing information, contact us (/about/contact) . Flagged listings are prioritized for re-verification.

Building trust, clarity, and practical tools for people navigating vision loss.

Low Vision Navigator exists because navigating low vision care is genuinely difficult. The path from a diagnosis to the right specialist, the right device, and the right funding is fragmented, inconsistent, and often invisible to the people who need it most.
We built Low Vision Navigator to change that. Our goal is a platform that gives patients a clear next step, gives clinicians a practical workflow, and gives caregivers the confidence to support—not just manage.

sections.heading: VisionServe Alliance
sections.text:
VisionServe Alliance is a consortium of 160+ US and Canadian organizations — including nonprofits, schools, rehabilitation centers, and employment agencies — collectively serving more than 150,000 people with blindness and low vision. Their member network spans rehabilitation therapy, orientation and mobility, assistive technology, employment support, guide dog services, and Braille production.
VisionServe Alliance operates VisionRefer , a free, HIPAA-compliant electronic referral system that connects eye care professionals to accredited vision rehabilitation providers. VisionRefer is currently active across 17+ states, with full coverage in Florida, Oklahoma, and Indiana. Clinicians can track referral status and receive progress updates while patients remain in the care of their referring provider.
VisionServe Alliance also leads the Aging and Vision Loss National Coalition (AVLNC) , a 160+ organization consortium advocating for increased access and quality of life for adults 65+ with vision loss. Key AVLNC initiatives include the Big Data Project — county- and state-level reports on vision impairment rates developed with The Ohio State University College of Optometry — and Teddie-Joy's Law , bipartisan federal legislation aimed at expanding community-based vision rehabilitation in underserved areas.
Visit VisionServe Alliance (https://visionservealliance.org) Learn about VisionRefer (https://visionservealliance.org/visionrefer/) About AVLNC (https://visionservealliance.org/aging-and-vision-loss/)

sections.heading: Intake questionnaire data
sections.text: Your intake questionnaire answers are stored only on your device using your browser's localStorage. They are never transmitted to our servers, never shared with third parties, and never used for advertising. You can delete this data at any time by clicking "Start Over" on the results page or clearing your browser's local storage.

sections.heading: AI assistant
sections.text: When you use the Ask the Assistant feature, your questions, the earlier messages in that conversation, and the address of the page you are on are sent to our AI provider, OpenAI, to generate an answer. We turn off OpenAI's option to save conversations, though OpenAI may keep request data for a limited time under its own policies. Answers may also search public websites. The conversation is kept in your browser only for the current tab and is erased when you close it. Please don't include personal details such as your full name, Social Security number, or medical record numbers. If you use voice input, your browser's built-in speech recognition converts your speech to text; depending on your browser, that audio may be processed by the browser maker's service. Read-aloud uses your device's built-in voices.

sections.heading: Analytics
sections.text: We collect anonymized, aggregated analytics to understand how the platform is used—which pages are most visited, how people navigate the intake flow, and where users encounter friction. This data does not include personally identifiable information.

sections.heading: What support looks like
sections.text: Caregiver support for vision loss includes respite services, education about vision conditions and rehabilitation, family counseling, and practical training in sighted guide techniques and home safety. Caring for someone with vision impairment can become all-consuming without structured boundaries and support. Many organizations offer caregiver-specific programs, peer groups, and phone-based counseling.

sections.text:
- Spouses, adult children, and partners of someone with vision loss

- Parents of children with visual impairments

- Caregivers experiencing stress, burnout, or overwhelm

- Family members who want to help but don't know how

- People navigating care responsibilities alongside work and family

sections.heading: Where to start
sections.text:
- Ask the person's eye care provider to include caregiver education at appointments

- Contact your state blind agency — many have caregiver programs

- Search for respite care through Area Agency on Aging (AAA) programs

- Learn sighted guide technique — a short training that immediately helps

- Connect with a peer caregiver support group through CNIB or AFB

sections.heading: What support looks like
sections.text: Educational support for students with visual impairments is provided through specialized professionals embedded in or consulting to the public school system. Under IDEA (Individuals with Disabilities Education Act), eligible students are entitled to a Free Appropriate Public Education (FAPE) with supports including Teacher of the Visually Impaired (TVI) services, O&M instruction, accessible materials, and assistive technology. Services are documented in an Individualized Education Program (IEP) or Section 504 plan.

sections.heading: Who it's for
sections.text:
- Students from birth through 21 with visual impairment or blindness

- Children with CVI, albinism, retinal disorders, or other vision conditions affecting learning

- Students with combined vision and other disabilities

- Families unsure whether their child qualifies for vision services

- Students transitioning to college or employment

sections.heading: Where to start
sections.text:
- Contact your school district's special education coordinator and request a vision evaluation

- Ask for a Functional Vision Assessment (FVA) and Learning Media Assessment (LMA)

- Request an IEP team meeting if your child already has an IEP

- Contact your state's school for the blind or vision services department for consultation

- Connect with the American Foundation for the Blind (AFB) FamilyConnect resource

sections.heading: Key questions to ask
sections.text:
Does my child qualify for TVI and O&M services under IDEA?
What is included in my child's IEP related to vision?
What accessible materials (Braille, large print, audio) are provided?
Is assistive technology evaluated and provided as part of the IEP?
How often does the TVI see my child, and what does instruction involve?

sections.heading: Emotional Support & Adjustment to Vision Loss
sections.text: Vision loss is a grief process. Counseling, peer support, and connection matter as much as clinical care.

sections.heading: What support looks like
sections.text: Emotional support for vision loss includes individual counseling, peer support groups (in-person and virtual), phone-based support lines, and structured adjustment programs. Many people describe the period after a significant diagnosis as involving stages of grief. Support helps people move toward acceptance and active adaptation—not by denying loss, but by building a new sense of possibility.

sections.heading: Who it's for
sections.text:
- Anyone newly diagnosed with a progressive or significant vision condition

- People experiencing depression, anxiety, or social isolation related to vision loss

- Caregivers and family members of someone with vision impairment

- Individuals who have lived with vision loss but never addressed the emotional impact

- People experiencing sudden vision loss (trauma, stroke, infection)

sections.heading: Where to start
sections.text:
- Ask your eye care provider for a referral to a social worker or counselor with vision loss experience

- Contact your state blind services agency—many have emotional support or peer programs

- Search the Association of Blindness Professionals (ABP) for peer specialists

- Contact VisionAware.org for self-directed resources and peer support directory

- Ask about tele-counseling if local services are limited

sections.heading: Key questions to ask
sections.text:

Are peer support groups available (in person or virtual)?
Is there a crisis or support line I can call when things are hard?

sections.text: Guide dog programs provide trained dogs, matched to individuals through a careful selection process, along with residential training (usually 2–4 weeks) at the school. - Applicants who can attend a residential training program (usually 2–4 weeks)

- Arrange for aftercare and veterinary support

sections.text: Support for older adults with vision loss addresses multiple intersecting needs: clinical care, rehabilitation, home safety, caregiver support, and social connection. Area Agencies on Aging, state blind agencies, and programs like VIST (for Veterans) provide structured support. - Families concerned about an aging parent's safety and independence

sections.heading: Appeals & Documentation
sections.text: Home (/) / Coverage & Funding (/coverage-funding) / Appeals

sections.heading: Appeals & Documentation
sections.text:
Most denials can be appealed. Good documentation dramatically improves approval odds.

This site helps organize next steps and local resources. It does not replace medical diagnosis, emergency care, or professional legal or insurance advice.

sections.heading: Before you appeal
sections.text: Request an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) and the specific denial reason in writing. Most denials state the payer's criteria—your appeal should address each criterion directly.

sections.heading: Functional impact statement
sections.text: Describe specific tasks the patient cannot do without the requested device or service. Quantify where possible (e.g., "reading speed reduced to 20 WPM without magnification").

sections.heading: Diagnosis and severity
sections.text: Include ICD-10 codes, best-corrected VA, and relevant functional test results. Contrast sensitivity and visual field data are often more compelling than acuity alone.

sections.heading: Alternatives tried and failed
sections.text: Document what was tried and why it was insufficient. This directly addresses "medical necessity" criteria.

sections.heading: Expected functional outcome
sections.text: State what function will be restored or preserved with the requested item. Tie it to goals—work, school, safety, or ADL independence.

sections.heading: The appeals process (Medicare and most private plans)
sections.text:
- 1 Request reconsideration within 60 days of the denial notice.

- 2 Submit updated documentation—add functional testing results and a revised LMN.

- 3 If denied again, request a Qualified Independent Contractor (QIC) review.

- 4 Request an ALJ (Administrative Law Judge) hearing if still denied.

- 5 Consider engaging a patient advocate, social worker, or disability attorney for complex cases.

Medicaid Buy-In programs exist in most states but their names, income limits, premium structures, and covered services vary significantly. Contact your state Medicaid agency to confirm program availability and current rules.

sections.text:
- Low vision exams and rehabilitation services (same coverage as standard Medicaid)

- Occupational therapy and vision rehabilitation therapy through Medicaid HCBS waivers

pages.title: Low Vision FAQ: Care, Coverage, Rehab & Technology
pages.description: Answers to the questions people ask most about low vision care, coverage, rehabilitation, and technology.

sections.heading: Low Vision FAQ: Care, Coverage, Rehab & Technology
sections.text:
Answers to the questions people ask most about low vision care, coverage, rehabilitation, and technology.

A regular eye exam focuses on diagnosing conditions and prescribing glasses or contacts. A low vision exam goes further—it evaluates how your remaining vision functions in real tasks like reading, cooking, or navigating outdoors. A low vision specialist tests contrast sensitivity, visual fields, glare tolerance, and reading speed, then recommends devices, lighting strategies, and rehabilitation services tailored to your goals.

Coverage varies significantly. Medicare typically covers the low vision exam under certain provider types but does not cover optical magnifiers or most electronic aids. Some Medicaid programs and state vocational rehabilitation agencies do cover devices. Veterans may qualify for devices through VA low vision programs. Private insurance is inconsistent—prior authorization and documentation of medical necessity are often required. Our Coverage & Funding section walks through options step by step.

It depends on your insurance and state. Many Medicare patients can self-refer to optometrists or ophthalmologists who specialize in low vision. Some insurance plans require a referral from a primary care provider or general eye doctor. Vocational rehabilitation and blind services agencies typically accept direct applications. When in doubt, call your insurer or the specialist's office directly—they can tell you exactly what documentation you need.

Students with visual impairments are entitled to a free, appropriate public education under IDEA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. A Teacher of the Visually Impaired (TVI) provides specialized instruction, and an Orientation & Mobility (O&M) specialist helps with safe navigation. Start by requesting an educational evaluation from your school district. Our School & Learning section has a checklist of what to ask for and how to advocate for the right services.

Orientation & Mobility (O&M) training teaches people with visual impairments to travel safely and independently. An O&M specialist works with you on techniques like using a white cane, navigating intersections, using public transit, and building mental maps of familiar routes. Sessions typically happen in real environments—your home, neighborhood, and workplace—so skills transfer immediately to daily life.

sections.heading: Low Vision FAQ: Care, Coverage, Rehab & Technology
sections.text:
The best reading tool depends on your vision level, task, and preferences. Optical magnifiers (handheld or stand) work well for quick tasks like price tags or labels. Desktop video magnifiers (CCTVs) are excellent for extended reading like books or mail. Screen readers and OCR apps can read text aloud from printed documents or screens. A vision rehabilitation therapist or assistive technology specialist can help you trial options before purchasing.

A Vision Rehabilitation Therapist (VRT) is a specialist trained to help people with vision loss learn or relearn daily living skills—cooking, medication management, labeling, financial tasks, and more. They also teach adaptive techniques for home safety and personal care. VRTs often work alongside low vision optometrists, O&M specialists, and occupational therapists. Referrals can come from eye care providers, state blind agencies, or hospital rehab programs.

Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) provides monthly benefits to people who have worked and paid into Social Security but can no longer perform substantial gainful activity due to a disability—including vision impairment. The SSA uses a "grid" of age, education, and work history to evaluate eligibility alongside medical evidence. Legal blindness (best-corrected VA of 20/200 or worse, or visual field of 20 degrees or less) has a specific listing. A benefits counselor or disability attorney can help you understand your options.

Possibly, depending on your state's visual acuity and field requirements. Many states allow driving with best-corrected acuity between 20/40 and 20/200 using bioptic telescopes—a specialized lens system mounted on eyeglasses. A certified driver rehabilitation specialist (CDRS) can evaluate your functional vision and recommend adaptive equipment or training. If driving is no longer safe, there are often funded transportation alternatives including paratransit, ride assistance programs, and volunteer driver networks.

A functional vision assessment (FVA) evaluates how a person uses their remaining vision in everyday tasks—not just how well they can read a chart. It measures things like reading speed and endurance, contrast sensitivity, near and distance task performance, lighting preferences, and visual fatigue. FVAs are performed by low vision specialists, vision rehabilitation therapists, or teachers of the visually impaired, and the results drive rehabilitation goals and device recommendations.

sections.heading: Low Vision FAQ: Care, Coverage, Rehab & Technology
sections.text:
State vocational rehabilitation (VR) agencies help people with disabilities—including low vision—prepare for, find, and keep employment. Services may include workplace accommodations, assistive technology funding, job coaching, training programs, and college tuition assistance. Blind Services agencies often provide expanded VR services specifically for people with visual impairments. Eligibility is based on having a disability that creates a barrier to employment, not on income. Contact your state's VR or Blind Services office to apply directly.

Medicaid Buy-In (also called Medicaid for Workers with Disabilities, or MWD) allows people with disabilities who are employed—or earning income—to pay a premium and keep Medicaid coverage at income levels that would normally disqualify them. This is important for people with low vision who want to work without losing access to Medicaid-funded therapies, devices, and services. Eligibility rules vary by state, including income limits and asset rules. Our Medicaid Buy-In page covers state-specific details.

Yes. Tele-rehabilitation for low vision expanded significantly and many providers now offer remote functional vision assessments, device training, orientation and mobility coaching (for home environments), and vision rehabilitation therapy via video. Some limitations apply—certain optical device prescriptions still require an in-person exam—but remote services are a strong option for people in rural areas or those with transportation barriers. Ask your state blind services agency or low vision clinic if they offer telehealth appointments.

The leading causes of low vision in adults are age-related macular degeneration (AMD), glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and cataracts that cannot be fully corrected surgically. Other causes include retinitis pigmentosa, optic nerve damage, stroke-related vision loss (hemianopia), and Stargardt disease (a hereditary macular condition). Each condition affects vision differently—AMD typically affects central vision, glaucoma affects peripheral vision, and hemianopia affects one side of the visual field—which is why tailored rehabilitation matters.

sections.heading: Low Vision FAQ: Care, Coverage, Rehab & Technology
sections.text:
Start with these directories: the American Academy of Optometry's "Find an Optometrist" tool (filter for low vision), the American Optometric Association locator, or the Vision Rehabilitation section of the American Academy of Ophthalmology. State blind services agencies maintain referral lists and can often provide a direct referral. Hospital-based low vision clinics at university medical centers frequently have experienced specialists. Ask any general eye doctor for a specific referral—not just a general ophthalmologist or optometrist—to someone who performs comprehensive low vision exams.

Lighting and contrast are among the lowest-cost, highest-impact interventions for people with low vision. Key strategies include: using task lighting directly on the work surface (not overhead only), choosing daylight-spectrum (5000–6500K) bulbs to improve color discrimination, increasing contrast by using dark plates on light tablecloths and vice versa, placing high-contrast tape or paint on steps and edges, and using large-print or high-contrast labeled items. A vision rehabilitation therapist can do a home assessment and make specific recommendations for your vision type and living situation.

Legal blindness is an administrative definition: best-corrected visual acuity of 20/200 or worse in the better eye, or a visual field of 20 degrees or less. It does not mean total darkness—most legally blind people have usable remaining vision. Legal blindness matters because it is the eligibility threshold for many federal and state benefit programs, including SSI, SSDI blind listings, IRS extra deductions, and some state blind services programs. Low vision is a broader functional term covering significant visual impairment that cannot be corrected, including many people who do not meet the legal blindness threshold but still face daily challenges.

Eccentric viewing (EV) is a technique used by people with central vision loss—such as from macular degeneration—to use a preferred retinal locus (PRL) in the peripheral retina instead of the damaged fovea. With training, the brain learns to direct gaze so that the PRL is positioned on a target, effectively "looking around" the blind spot. Research shows EV training significantly improves reading speed and task performance. It is taught by vision rehabilitation therapists and low vision specialists, and typically takes several weeks of guided practice to become automatic.

sections.heading: State Blind Agencies & Commissions
sections.text:
Federally funded state programs that provide free or low-cost rehabilitation, training, technology, and financial support for people with visual impairments.

Every US state has a state agency for the blind or a division of vocational rehabilitation that serves people with visual impairments. These agencies are funded through a combination of state and federal money (Titles I and VII of the Rehabilitation Act) and provide services at no charge to eligible individuals.

sections.heading: Vocational Rehabilitation (VR)
sections.text: Job training, workplace accommodations, assistive technology for employment, and job placement support. Often no cost to eligible individuals.

sections.heading: Independent Living Services
sections.text: Orientation & mobility training, ADL (daily living skills) training, and home modification assessments for non-vocational goals. Older individuals with vision loss are a priority population.

sections.heading: Assistive Technology
sections.text: Free short-term device loans, technology assessments, and purchasing assistance for computers, screen readers, magnification software, CCTVs, and other aids.

sections.heading: Low Vision Clinic Referrals
sections.text: Many state agencies maintain referral relationships with low vision clinics and can coordinate examinations for eligible individuals.

sections.heading: Transition Services
sections.text: Support for students with visual impairments transitioning to work, post-secondary education, or independent living.

sections.heading: Braille & Literacy
sections.text: Braille instruction, reading materials in accessible formats (braille, large print, audio), and talking book library access (NLS).

sections.heading: How to apply
sections.text:
- 1 Search "[Your State] state agency for the blind" or "[Your State] division of vocational rehabilitation" to find the correct agency. Some states have separate agencies for blindness; others fold vision services into a general VR agency.

- 2 Call or submit an online application. No referral is needed — you apply directly. Bring documentation of your vision diagnosis (ophthalmologist or optometrist records).

- 3 An eligibility determination will be made, usually within 60 days. If eligible, a counselor will develop an Individualized Plan for Employment (IPE) or Independent Living Plan with you.

- 4 Services begin based on your plan. Priority is given to people with the most significant disabilities when funding is limited — legal blindness typically qualifies as a significant disability.

sections.heading: Order of selection (when funding is limited)
sections.text:
When state VR agencies have more applicants than funding allows, they implement an "order of selection" that prioritizes individuals with the most significant disabilities. Legal blindness almost always qualifies for the highest priority category. If your state is in order of selection, ask to be placed on the waiting list and ask what interim services may still be available.

sections.heading: Common Medicare denial reasons
sections.text:
Denial reason: Refraction billed to Medicare Part B
Refraction is a statutory non-covered service under Medicare. Bill separately to patient or supplemental plan, or have patient sign ABN.

Denial reason: Optical low vision devices billed to Medicare
Medicare does not cover optical aids (magnifiers, telescopes, bioptics). Document and inform patient upfront; refer to VR or state blind agency for funding.

Denial reason: Lack of medical necessity documentation
Include functional impact on daily activities. Document specific tasks affected (reading medication labels, driving, cooking) and link to diagnosis with ICD-10 code.

Denial reason: Exceeding therapy cap without exception
Use KX modifier to bypass cap when services are medically necessary and documented. Annual therapy cap applies unless exceptions apply.

Denial reason: "Not a covered benefit" for assistive technology
Most electronic low vision aids are not covered by Medicare. Refer to VA (for veterans), state VR, or Medicaid Waiver programs for alternative funding.

sections.heading: Problem-oriented approach
sections.text:
Start with the patient's stated functional concerns. Use the core domains below to build a targeted assessment plan—not a full battery for every patient. Each domain links to test options, red flags, and how findings shape device and referral recommendations.
View test selection recipes by patient type (/professionals/test-selection-recipes)
Visual Acuity The foundation of any low vision assessment. Measures best-corrected distance and near acuity using standardized charts. ETDRS chart Snellen chart Feinbloom chart Near acuity card (/professionals/diagnostic-resources/core-domains#visual-acuity) Visual Fields Peripheral and central field integrity affects mobility, driving, reading, and overall function. Confrontation testing Amsler grid Humphrey visual field Goldmann perimetry (/professionals/diagnostic-resources/core-domains#visual-fields) Contrast Sensitivity Often more predictive of real-world function than acuity alone. Impacts reading, face recognition, and step detection. Pelli-Robson chart Mars Letter CS test CSV-1000 FACT chart (/professionals/diagnostic-resources/core-domains#contrast-sensitivity) Glare & Light Sensitivity Significant functional impact for many conditions. Guides filter selection and environmental recommendations. BAT (Brightness Acuity Tester) Glare disability testing Photophobia history Filter trial (/professionals/diagnostic-resources/core-domains#glare-light-sensitivity) Oculomotor Function Fixation stability, eccentric viewing ability, and scanning patterns directly affect reading and device success. Fixation stability assessment Preferred Retinal Locus (PRL) Saccadic tracking Reading performance testing (/professionals/diagnostic-resources/core-domains#oculomotor-function) Cognitive Status Learning capacity, memory, and executive function affect training success and device adoption. MoCA screen MMSE Clinical observation Goal-setting interview (/professionals/diagnostic-resources/core-domains#cognitive-status) Functional Goals Patient-centered priorities drive test selection, device choice, and outcome measurement. VA LV VFQ-48 IVI questionnaire Goal Attainment Scaling Structured interview (/professionals/diagnostic-resources/core-domains#functional-goals) Environment & Task Demands Lighting, task distances, and environmental complexity inform practical recommendations. Task analysis Environmental assessment Occupational profile Home visit (/professionals/diagnostic-resources/core-domains#environment-task-demands) Manual Dexterity & Handling Affects device selection and usability—particularly for optical devices and Braille tools. Fine motor observation Grip strength screen Device handling trial OT consultation (/professionals/diagnostic-resources/core-domains#manual-dexterity)

View steps Collapse

sections.text: When to refer, who to refer to, and what to include in your referral.

sections.heading: Orientation & Mobility Specialist
sections.text:
Refer when:

- Falls history or fear of falling

- Difficulty with street crossings, stairs, or transit

- Visual field loss ≥30° or VA ≤20/200

- Patient lives alone

- Wants to use public transportation independently

Clinical note
Priority referral. Do not wait until device training is complete.

sections.heading: Vision Rehabilitation Therapist (VRT)
sections.text:
Refer when:

- Difficulty with reading, cooking, medication management

- Home safety concerns

- ADL independence goals

- New to significant vision loss

Clinical note
Can often provide home visits. State blind agencies frequently employ or fund VRTs.

sections.heading: Occupational Therapist (OT) — Vision Specialty
sections.text:
Refer when:

- Work-related goals

- Complex ADL needs

- Cognitive overlay

- Post-acute rehabilitation context

Clinical note
Ensure OT has vision specialization; general OTs may lack low vision training.

sections.heading: Teacher of the Visually Impaired (TVI)
sections.text:
Refer when:

- School-age patient

- IEP or 504 plan needed

- Braille literacy or accessible materials assessment

- Learning media assessment (LMA) needed

Clinical note
Refer to school district special education coordinator. TVI can evaluate and serve on IEP team.

sections.heading: Assistive Technology Specialist
sections.text:
Refer when:

- Computer or workplace AT needs

- Screen reader or magnification software instruction needed

- Complex device needs beyond optical devices

Clinical note
State AT programs offer free evaluations and device trials. AER and ATIA certify AT specialists.

sections.heading: Social Work / Care Coordination
sections.text:
Refer when:

- Financial barriers to care

- Social isolation or depression

- Housing instability

- Caregiver burden concerns

- Benefits navigation needed

Clinical note
Often the most underused referral. Significant unmet need in most low vision practices.

sections.heading: Neuro-Ophthalmology
sections.text:
Refer when:

- Suspected CVI (cortical visual impairment)

- Optic neuropathy of unclear etiology

- Visual field defect with possible neurological origin

- Incongruent acuity and visual field findings

Clinical note
Required for complete workup when clinical picture doesn't fit. Affects both prognosis and rehab planning.

sections.heading: Electronic referrals via VisionRefer
sections.text:
VisionRefer is a free, HIPAA-compliant electronic referral platform operated by VisionServe Alliance that connects eye care and medical professionals to accredited vision rehabilitation providers. Once a referral is submitted, the referring clinician receives status updates as the patient progresses — while the patient remains under their care.

- Active in 17+ states; full county coverage in Florida, Oklahoma, and Indiana

- Only VisionServe Alliance accredited member agencies can receive referrals

- Free for referring providers and patients

- Tracks referral status so you can follow patient progress

Learn about VisionRefer (https://visionservealliance.org/visionrefer/)

sections.heading: Research & Evidence Base for Low Vision Rehabilitation
sections.text:
Key studies, systematic reviews, and clinical practice guidelines supporting evidence-based low vision rehabilitation.

Low vision rehabilitation has a growing evidence base, but access to that evidence is scattered across ophthalmology, optometry, occupational therapy, and rehabilitation medicine literature. This page collects the most clinically relevant findings for practitioners.

sections.heading: LIVEMD (Low Vision Intervention Trial)
sections.text:
Randomized trial demonstrating statistically significant improvements in visual acuity, reading, and quality of life with structured low vision rehabilitation. Key evidence for comprehensive rehab model.
JAMA Ophthalmology, 2018

sections.heading: National Eye Institute Low Vision Education Program Research
sections.text:
Population-level data on unmet rehabilitation needs. Found that fewer than 10% of people with low vision who could benefit from rehabilitation are referred to services.
NEI, ongoing

sections.heading: Impact of Low Vision Rehabilitation on VA/VFQ-25 Outcomes
sections.text:
Multiple studies show statistically significant improvements on the Visual Function Questionnaire-25 following structured O&M and ADL rehabilitation, with sustained gains at 6-month follow-up.
Ophthalmology, multiple years

sections.heading: Eccentric Viewing Training Outcomes
sections.text:
Systematic review showing eccentric viewing training significantly improves reading speed and accuracy in patients with central scotomas (AMD, Stargardt). Most benefit seen with specialist-guided practice.
Cochrane Reviews / IOVS

sections.heading: Tele-Rehabilitation for Low Vision: Feasibility and Outcomes
sections.text:
Post-pandemic research demonstrating non-inferiority of tele-rehabilitation to in-person for ADL and reading outcomes, with superior access for rural and mobility-limited populations.
Optometry and Vision Science, 2021–2023

sections.heading: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Low Vision Rehabilitation
sections.text:
The most comprehensive evidence-based clinical guideline for low vision rehabilitation in the US. Covers assessment, intervention, AT, and follow-up. Freely available.
healthquality.va.gov
AAO

sections.heading: Preferred Practice Pattern: Vision Rehabilitation
sections.text:
American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP for vision rehabilitation, including low vision services. Updated periodically; provides referral and co-management guidance.
aao.org
AOTA

sections.heading: Low Vision and Blindness: Occupational Therapy Practice Guidelines
sections.text:
Evidence-based practice guidelines for OT in low vision. Includes intervention descriptions, outcome measures, and evidence ratings.
aota.org

sections.heading: VFQ-25 (Visual Function Questionnaire)
sections.text: NEI validated patient-reported outcome measure; 25-item subscales for near/distance activities, social function, and mental health.

sections.heading: MNREAD Acuity Chart
sections.text: Standardized reading speed assessment; used to measure eccentric viewing and magnification outcomes.

sections.heading: Melbourne Low-Vision ADL Index (MLVAI)
sections.text: Performance-based ADL assessment validated for low vision populations.

sections.heading: IVI (Impact of Vision Impairment)

Self-report measure capturing emotional, daily activity, and social participation impact of low vision.

sections.heading: ADL Training & Occupational Therapy
sections.text: Relearning daily tasks—cooking, medications, home safety—with adaptive techniques matched to your vision.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Activities of Daily Living (ADL) training helps people with vision loss safely and efficiently manage everyday tasks. Vision Rehabilitation Therapists (VRTs) and occupational therapists (OTs) specializing in vision teach adaptive strategies and use specialized tools to restore independence in cooking, personal care, home management, and medication management.

sections.heading: Who it helps
sections.text:
- Adults who have experienced vision loss affecting daily tasks

- Seniors at risk for medication errors, kitchen accidents, or falls

- Individuals with severe or profound vision loss beginning rehabilitation

- People who have had vision loss for years but never received formal training

- Caregivers learning to support without creating dependency

sections.heading: Common goals
sections.text:
- Safe, independent meal preparation and cooking

- Accurate medication identification and self-administration

- Personal care: grooming, hygiene, dressing organization

- Home organization and labeling systems

- Mail, financial tasks, and paperwork management

- Safe movement within the home

sections.heading: What sessions may involve
sections.text:
Task analysis of current routines
Adaptive cooking techniques and kitchen safety
Talking tools and tactile labeling
Clothing organization and identification strategies
Bill paying and financial management adaptations
Home environment assessment and modification recommendations

sections.heading: How to access it
sections.text: VRTs work through state blind services agencies, hospital and clinic-based rehabilitation programs, and VA low vision programs. Occupational therapists with vision specialization can be found through rehabilitation hospitals and some home health agencies. State blind agencies often provide VRT services at no cost to qualifying clients.

sections.heading: Assistive Technology Instruction
sections.text: Device success depends on training—not just the device. Structured instruction makes the difference.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Assistive technology instruction teaches people with visual impairments to use adaptive devices and software effectively. Getting the right device is only part of the solution—most people need structured training to build the skills, confidence, and habits that lead to real-world use. AT instruction is provided by certified assistive technology professionals (ATPs), TVIs, VRTs, and rehabilitation technology specialists.

sections.heading: Who it helps
sections.text:
- Anyone who has received a device but struggles to use it consistently

- People new to screen readers, magnification software, or OCR apps

- Individuals transitioning to new technology platforms

- Students and working adults needing efficient tech workflows

- Seniors learning to use smartphones or tablets for accessibility

sections.heading: Common goals
sections.text:
- Efficient use of screen magnification or screen reader software

- Smartphone and tablet accessibility feature mastery

- OCR and scanning app proficiency for mail and documents

- Video magnifier operation for reading and tasks

- Integration of multiple tools into daily workflows

sections.heading: What sessions may involve
sections.text:
Device setup and configuration for visual needs
Systematic feature introduction and practice
Workflow development for common tasks (email, reading, navigation)
Keyboard shortcut training (for screen reader users)
Problem-solving and troubleshooting strategies
Follow-up check-ins to reinforce skill retention

sections.heading: How to access it
sections.text: AT instruction is available through state blind agencies (often free), assistive technology programs (check the AT3 Center directory), VA VIST programs, and some low vision clinics. The AER directory lists providers by specialization.

sections.heading: Functional Vision Assessment
sections.text: A real-world evaluation that goes beyond the exam lane to understand how vision affects daily life.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: A Functional Vision Assessment (FVA) evaluates how a person uses their vision in real-world conditions—not just under standardized clinical testing. It examines how vision performs in variable lighting, at task-relevant distances, and for specific daily activities like reading, cooking, or navigating outdoors. FVAs are used by low vision specialists, TVIs, VRTs, and O&M specialists to guide rehabilitation planning.

sections.heading: Who it helps
sections.text:
- Anyone preparing for a rehabilitation plan

- Students where a Learning Media Assessment is needed

- Adults with complex or variable vision loss

- Individuals whose clinical acuity doesn't match their reported functional difficulty

- People with CVI (Cortical Visual Impairment) where standard testing may be unreliable

sections.heading: Common goals
sections.text:
- Identify most limiting functional challenges

- Determine best corrected vision for near, intermediate, and distance tasks

- Assess how lighting and contrast affect performance

- Identify preferred retinal locus (PRL) for reading

- Guide device selection and trial priorities

sections.heading: What sessions may involve
sections.text:
Task performance observation in natural conditions
Lighting variation assessment
Near, intermediate, and distance task simulation
Reading performance testing
Glare tolerance assessment
Technology and device handling observation

sections.heading: How to access it
sections.text: Functional vision assessments are performed by low vision optometrists, ophthalmologists, TVIs (for students), and VRTs. Referrals often come from primary eye care providers or state blind agencies. For school-age children, an FVA is often part of the educational evaluation process under IDEA.

sections.heading: Home Modifications & Lighting
sections.text: Simple changes with outsized impact on safety, independence, and daily ease.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Home modifications for vision loss focus on maximizing the use of remaining vision and reducing hazards. Unlike physical accessibility modifications, most vision-related home changes involve lighting optimization, contrast enhancement, organization, and labeling—many of which can be done at low or no cost. A vision rehabilitation therapist or OT can conduct a home visit assessment.

sections.heading: Who it helps
sections.text:
- Anyone with vision loss who spends significant time at home

- Seniors at elevated risk for falls or medication errors

- People with glare sensitivity or light adaptation difficulties

- Caregivers wanting to create a safer, more independent home environment

- Individuals transitioning from the hospital or a care facility to home

sections.heading: Common goals
sections.text:
- Reduce fall risk through contrast marking and clutter reduction

- Optimize task lighting for reading, cooking, and self-care

- Establish organized systems for medications and daily items

- Mark hazards (stairs, stove dials, appliance controls)

- Create a home environment that supports maximum independence

sections.heading: What sessions may involve
sections.text:
Room-by-room lighting assessment and recommendations
Contrast tape application on stairs and step edges
Medication organization and labeling systems
Kitchen safety modifications and tool organization
Appliance marking with tactile or hi-contrast labels
Clutter reduction and consistent placement strategies

sections.heading: How to access it
sections.text: Home assessments are conducted by VRTs, OTs with vision specialization, and O&M specialists. State blind agencies often provide this service at no cost. Some community programs and Area Agencies on Aging also offer home modification services.

sections.heading: Orientation & Mobility Training
sections.text: Teaching safe, independent travel for people with visual impairments—from home to community and beyond.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Orientation & Mobility (O&M) is a specialized rehabilitation discipline that teaches people with visual impairments to travel safely and independently. O&M specialists are certified professionals who work with clients in real environments—not just clinics—to develop practical travel skills using structured techniques and tools like the white cane or guide dog.

sections.heading: Who it helps
sections.text:
- Adults and children with any level of vision loss affecting travel

- People with fear of falling or recent falls history

- Individuals who have stopped leaving home due to vision changes

- Students needing to navigate school and community environments

- Newly visually impaired adults adapting to significant vision changes

sections.heading: Common goals
sections.text:
- Safe travel within the home

- Independent outdoor travel including curbs and intersections

- Using public transit independently

- Shopping, medical appointments, and community access

- Developing mental mapping skills for familiar routes

- Learning to use a white cane effectively

sections.heading: What sessions may involve
sections.text:
Cane technique (straight-line, touch, and diagonal methods)
Environmental orientation and spatial reasoning
Intersection analysis and crossing strategies
Bus, subway, and rideshare navigation
Sighted guide techniques (taught to companions)
Problem-solving in unfamiliar environments

sections.heading: How to access it
sections.text: O&M specialists can be found through state blind services agencies, school districts (for students), VA low vision programs, and some low vision clinics and hospitals. Referrals from eye care providers, state agencies, or vocational rehabilitation programs are common pathways. Funding is often available through state blind agencies at no cost to the client.

sections.heading: Tele-Rehab Options
sections.text: Remote vision rehabilitation services for when travel is difficult or specialty care isn't local.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Tele-rehabilitation (tele-rehab) delivers vision rehabilitation services via video call, phone, or remote monitoring technology. While not all services can be delivered remotely, many VRT, AT instruction, and follow-up sessions are highly effective in a virtual format. Tele-rehab has expanded access significantly, particularly for people in rural areas or those with mobility limitations.

sections.heading: Who it helps
sections.text:
- People in rural or underserved areas with limited local specialists

- Individuals with mobility limitations or transportation barriers

- Follow-up sessions after initial in-person evaluation

- Family and caregiver training

- AT instruction that can be done via screen sharing

sections.heading: Common goals
sections.text:
- Receive rehabilitation guidance without long-distance travel

- Continue services between in-person appointments

- Access specialty providers not available locally

- Receive AT instruction via screen sharing

- Caregiver training and family education

sections.heading: What sessions may involve
sections.text:
Video-based skills instruction and coaching
Screen sharing for AT instruction (ZoomText, JAWS, etc.)
Environmental assessment via video walk-through
Goal review and progress monitoring
Family and caregiver education
Resource and referral guidance

sections.heading: How to access it
sections.text: Ask your state blind agency, local low vision clinic, or VRT provider if they offer virtual services. Many expanded tele-services during COVID-19 and have maintained them. Some national organizations (CNIB, Lighthouse Guild) offer virtual programs. The VIST program at VA also provides tele-health services.

sections.heading: Visual Skills Training
sections.text: Home (/) / Rehab & Training (/rehab-training) / Visual Skills Training

sections.heading: Visual Skills Training
sections.text: Training techniques that improve how you use your remaining vision—not the vision itself.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Visual skills training teaches people with low vision to use their remaining sight more effectively. Key techniques include eccentric viewing (using peripheral retina for central tasks in macular conditions), scanning training (systematic visual search strategies), and tracking (following moving targets). This training is distinct from vision therapy—it works with what remains, not to restore what is lost.

sections.heading: Who it helps
sections.text:
- People with macular degeneration or other central field loss

- Individuals who have struggled with magnification devices despite adequate power

- People who read slowly even with appropriate magnification

- Anyone with nystagmus or fixation instability

- Individuals with visual processing changes (CVI, TBI)

sections.heading: Common goals
sections.text:
- Develop a reliable Preferred Retinal Locus (PRL) for reading

- Improve reading speed and endurance with eccentric viewing

- Develop efficient scanning strategies for visual search

- Improve ability to track moving objects

- Integrate visual skills with device use

sections.heading: What sessions may involve
sections.text:
PRL identification and stability training
Eccentric viewing direction training
Reading drills with progressive print sizes
Scanning pattern development
Real-world task practice integrating trained skills
Computer-based training programs (where available)

sections.heading: How to access it
sections.text: Visual skills training is provided by low vision optometrists, vision rehabilitation therapists, and some occupational therapists with vision specialization. It is often integrated into a broader low vision rehabilitation program. Referrals through state blind agencies or low vision clinics.

sections.heading: What is low vision?
sections.text:
Low vision is a significant visual impairment that cannot be fully corrected with glasses, contact lenses, medication, or surgery. It's not blindness—most people with low vision have some usable sight.
Low vision is defined as best-corrected visual acuity of 20/70 or worse in the better eye, OR significant visual field loss. But definitions matter less than function—what you can and can't do in daily life.
Learn more about low vision (/start-here/what-is-low-vision)

sections.heading: How care usually works
sections.text:
- 1 Comprehensive eye exam identifies the condition

- 2 Low vision exam assesses functional vision

- 3 Rehabilitation evaluation sets goals

- 4 Training begins (O&M, VRT, AT)

- 5 Ongoing support and follow-up

sections.heading: Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)
sections.text: Central vision loss affecting reading, faces, and fine detail. Most common cause of low vision in adults over 60.

sections.heading: Glaucoma
sections.text: Progressive peripheral field loss that can narrow to tunnel vision over time. Often silent in early stages.

sections.heading: Diabetic Retinopathy
sections.text: Vision loss from damaged retinal blood vessels. Can cause fluctuating, scattered, or severe vision loss.

sections.heading: Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP)
sections.text: Progressive peripheral and night vision loss. Often begins in childhood or young adulthood.

sections.heading: Cortical Visual Impairment (CVI)
sections.text: Vision difficulty caused by brain processing differences rather than eye structure. Common in children with neurological conditions.

sections.text:

pages.title: Your First Next Steps After a Low Vision Diagnosis
pages.description: A practical guide to the first actions after learning you have low vision — from finding a specialist to exploring rehabilitation, devices, and funding options.

sections.heading: Schedule a low vision examination
sections.text:
Look for a low vision optometrist, ophthalmologist, or clinic that specializes in low vision—not just general eye care. Bring a list of tasks that are difficult. Expect the appointment to take 1–2 hours.

2

sections.heading: Contact your state blind services agency
sections.text:
Most states offer free or low-cost O&M training, rehabilitation therapy, and assistive technology through their blind services agency. No referral needed in most states—you can apply directly.

3

sections.heading: Learn what rehabilitation looks like
sections.text:
Rehabilitation is not just for dramatic vision loss. If vision is affecting any daily task—reading, cooking, mobility, work—rehabilitation can help. Start with a functional vision assessment.

4

sections.heading: Explore assistive device options
sections.text:
Don't buy devices online without trying them first. State AT programs offer free demonstrations and short-term loans. A low vision specialist can recommend the right magnification level for your specific tasks.

5

sections.heading: Map your coverage and funding options
sections.text:
Services and devices are often funded through state agencies, vocational rehabilitation, VA programs, or insurance. Use our Coverage & Funding section to find what applies to your situation.

6

sections.heading: Connect with community and peer support
sections.text: Talking with others who have navigated vision loss can be one of the most practical resources. Peer support programs, vision loss organizations, and online communities can reduce isolation and provide real-world advice.

sections.heading: What Is Low Vision?

sections.heading: What Is Low Vision?
sections.text:
Low vision is a significant visual impairment that cannot be fully corrected with glasses, contact lenses, medication, or surgery—but is not total blindness.
Most people with low vision have some usable sight. The clinical definition typically includes best-corrected visual acuity of 20/70 or worse in the better eye, or significant visual field loss (a reduced area of sight). But definitions matter less than function— what you can and can't do in daily life .

sections.heading: What it is NOT
sections.text:
- It is not blindness (though some people with "low vision" have very limited sight)

- It is not fixable with better glasses in most cases

- It is not a diagnosis—it describes functional impact across many conditions

- It is not a reason to stop doing the things that matter to you

sections.heading: Diagnosis does not equal prognosis
sections.text: Having a condition like macular degeneration or glaucoma does not mean you will lose all functional vision. Many people live active, independent lives with low vision using the right tools, training, and supports. Early rehabilitation significantly improves outcomes.

sections.heading: Legal blindness
sections.text: Legal blindness is defined as best-corrected VA of 20/200 or worse in the better eye, or a visual field of 20 degrees or less. Legal blindness is an administrative and legal category—it does not mean total loss of sight and does not require total darkness to qualify for services.
